transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Well, what brings me in is that I just... I can't keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. Even when it's really important. Like, I'll start tracing a client's network problem at work—I do computer support—and I'll be looking at the server logs. 

Which, by the way, the new logging software they pushed out to us last week is just terrible. It's got this awful dark mode default that you can't even turn off, and it makes my eyes water. I was actually complaining to my wife, Linda, about it over dinner on Tuesday. We had meatloaf, her mother's recipe with that sweet ketchup glaze... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, the network problem. So I'll be trying to trace the issue, and ten minutes later I'll realize I've reread the exact same log entries three times and I still have absolutely no idea what they actually say. It's just getting really bad.
Have you noticed this kind of trouble concentrating and getting sidetracked for most of your life, even back in school, or is this something that started more recently?

Yeah, oh, absolutely. It's... it's been forever. My mother actually still jokes about it. She says that back in grade school, my report cards always said the exact same thing—that I was bright, but I could never just stay in my seat. And I was always blurting out answers before the teacher even finished asking the question. Plus, I'd lose my homework all the time, even when I actually did it! 

Which reminds me, I was helping my grandson with his homework last weekend—he's in fourth grade now, doing this new math stuff. Have you seen how they teach math these days? It's completely different from how we learned it. They draw all these boxes and arrows, and it takes ten minutes to do a simple multiplication problem. I was trying to show him the way I learned it, just carrying the one, you know? But he got so frustrated because his teacher said he had to show the "area model" or whatever it's called. We ended up just taking a break and getting ice cream. We went to that little shop on Main Street, the one with the really good mint chocolate chip... but yeah, anyway, school was always like that for me. Always losing things and getting up when I wasn't supposed to.
Would you say these attention and distractibility problems are currently causing real difficulties for you both at work and at home, not just occasionally but on a regular basis?

Yeah, it's... it's really bad right now. Both places, work and home. It's actually why I'm here. See, I used to work for this big corporate IT department, and they had a whole ticketing system. Everything was structured, you know? But since I lost that job and started doing freelance and contract work... man, my reputation has just taken a massive hit. 

I've lost freelance clients because I just can't seem to get things done on time, or I forget a step. And I actually missed out on this senior service-manager role I applied for. The guy interviewing me was wearing this really interesting tie, actually. It had these little circuit boards printed on it, but if you looked closely, the lines made out the shape of a dog. I asked him where he got it, and he said his daughter bought it for him in Seattle. I've always wanted to visit Seattle, see the Space Needle and all that. Linda and I talked about going for our anniversary, but... well, that's the other thing.

Because I keep losing clients and missing out on jobs, Linda and I have been really worried about money lately. It's putting a lot of strain on us at home. People just don't trust me to follow through anymore, and it's... it's just really hard.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports lifelong (childhood-onset) symptoms of inattention (losing items, difficulty sustaining focus, rereading material without comprehension, forgetfulness) and hyperactive-impulsive traits (unable to stay seated, blurting answers) documented since grade school per report cards and parental observation. Symptoms persist into adulthood with clear functional impairment across multiple settings—occupational (job loss, failed interview, lost freelance clients) and interpersonal/financial (marital strain over money). Additionally, the patient's speech during the interview demonstrates marked tangentiality and distractibility (frequent unprompted digressions about logging software, meatloaf, math homework, ties, Seattle), consistent with an attention-deficit presentation rather than a primary mood, anxiety, or thought disorder. No evidence of manic/psychotic symptoms, and mood complaints are secondary to functional impairment rather than primary. This supports ADHD, combined presentation.
